annotationRationale: The question tests applying a discount and recovering an original price after successive percentage changes. Computing a percentage supports the tax calculation. The supplied approaches share this same short calculation, so a separate rearrangement would not add a distinct method.

review.questionCheck: The final cost is 0.8·1.075=0.86 times the original price, so the budget permits original prices up to 50 dollars. At 50 dollars, the discounted price is 40 dollars and tax is 3 dollars. B is correct; supplied statements and choices agree.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The references use the same short percentage calculation or verify the largest choice. A separate rearrangement or guess-and-check route is unnecessary.
review.annotationCheck: Discounts and recovering a whole from its percentage are appropriate assessed concepts. Percentage-of-a-number supports the tax calculation.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The discount leaves 0.8p, and tax on that amount produces 1.075·0.8p=0.86p. Since this coefficient is positive, affordability is equivalent to p≤50. Equality is attainable, establishing the requested maximum.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: LIVE and the supplied AoPS percentage solutions support the multiplier-and-budget route. The candidate uses original explanatory prose, correctly identifies third-party influence, and makes no official MAA claim.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The explanation identifies the tax base, explains both multipliers, and checks the affordable boundary. A learner can reconstruct the calculation and understand why 50 dollars is the maximum.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_p203 captures the discount, cnm_p196 the tax percentage, and cnm_p198 recovery of the original price from the combined percentage. All immediate IDs are supported.
